title: Before It Was Too Late
paragraphs: Daniyar Bekmuratov had been thinking about his grandfather for weeks before he finally bought the train ticket. He had told himself that he was too busy, that the semester would end soon enough, that he would visit properly during the holidays. But one evening in October, as he was reading in his dormitory room, he put down his book, looked at the ceiling, and thought: if not now, when? He had been putting it off for months. He bought the ticket the next morning.

His grandfather, Seitkali-ata, was eighty-one years old and lived alone in a small house in Aktobe. He had worked all his life as a schoolteacher and had retired twenty-three years before Daniyar was born. He had married twice — his first wife had died of tuberculosis when his children were young, and he had raised them alone for seven years before meeting Daniyar's grandmother. He was a quiet man who had seen a great deal of the Soviet Union's history from a very particular vantage point: a one-room schoolhouse in the Kazakh steppe.

Daniyar arrived on a Thursday afternoon. His grandfather had been waiting by the window for an hour before the bus appeared. When Daniyar walked through the door, the old man stood up slowly and held his shoulders and looked at him for a long time before saying anything. Then: "You look like your mother when she was young." It was the nicest thing anyone had said to Daniyar in months.

They spent four days together. Seitkali-ata told stories Daniyar had never heard — about the famine years, about a student who had walked forty kilometres to school in 1961, about a winter so cold that the ink in the pens froze in the classroom. He told them without drama, in the same tone he might use to describe the weather. Daniyar listened and asked questions and wrote some of them down in his notebook, because he had a feeling, which he could not have put into words, that the time for hearing these stories was running out.

On the last morning, his grandfather asked: "Do you have everything you need at university?" Daniyar said yes. His grandfather nodded. Then he said: "Good. Work hard. And come back before it gets too cold." It was not a dramatic farewell. It was the farewell of a man who had learned, over eighty-one years, not to use unnecessary words.

Daniyar cried on the train home. Not because anything dramatic had happened, but because he suddenly understood something he had not understood before the visit: that his grandfather was one of the last living connections to a world that had passed, and that one day — perhaps not soon, but one day — he would no longer be there. The train passed through the steppe in the failing autumn light, and Daniyar wrote in his notebook: "I'm glad I came when I did."

He has gone back twice since. He went again in December, and again in the spring. He has been recording his grandfather's stories. He does not know how many more chances he will have. He is taking each one.

dialogue.speaker: Daniyar
dialogue.text: I almost didn't go. I kept telling myself I was too busy.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: What made you finally decide to buy the ticket?

dialogue.speaker: Daniyar
dialogue.text: I just thought — if not now, when? He's eighty-one. He had been waiting for me to visit for months.

dialogue.speaker: Daniyar
dialogue.text: More than anything I've done this semester. He told me stories I'd never heard. Things I had no idea about.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: Are you going to write them down?

dialogue.speaker: Daniyar
dialogue.text: I already have. I had been writing during the visit. I'm going to keep recording them.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: Good. Those stories matter. Don't let them disappear.

keyPhrases.context: "He had been putting it off for months." — action before another past moment.
"A very particular vantage point." = unique perspective or position.
"He told them without drama." = calmly, not dramatically.
"The time for hearing these stories was running out." = there was less and less time left.
"It was not a dramatic farewell." = the goodbye at the end of the visit.
"The failing autumn light." = the light growing dim as evening comes.
"Died of tuberculosis." — a serious lung disease, common in the Soviet era.

vocab.definition: a severe shortage of food affecting a large area
vocab.example: "Stories about the famine years." — periods of extreme food shortage.

vocab.definition: a place or position that gives a good view; a perspective
vocab.example: "From a very particular vantage point." — his unique perspective as a rural schoolteacher.

vocab.definition: a goodbye, especially when parting for a long time
vocab.example: "It was not a dramatic farewell." — the last morning goodbye.

vocab.definition: a serious infectious disease affecting the lungs
vocab.example: "His first wife had died of tuberculosis." — a common disease in Soviet-era Kazakhstan.

vocab.definition: a large area of flat, treeless grassland
vocab.example: "A one-room schoolhouse in the Kazakh steppe." — the open grasslands of Kazakhstan.

vocab.definition: striking and impressive; full of emotion
vocab.example: "He told them without drama." / "Not a dramatic farewell."

vocab.definition: one of two periods that the academic year is divided into
vocab.example: "The semester would end soon enough." — the half-year academic period.
"A very particular vantage point." — a specific, distinctive perspective.
